chapter: Flip Benson, Grand Rapids and the Army
title: Army Air Force service and first meeting with bebop
summary: Ware serves as a combat engineer from 1943 to 1946, avoids the base band, goes to the Pacific, and meets musicians who play the new music.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: You were 20 years old at that point.
And what was your musical involvement in the army?

Well, when we went through our basic, we had 45 musicians and I didn't read, so I wasn't even apt to get in the army band or the post band or anything like that. But all these musicians -- they were just making up battalions; like I said, we were in the Army Air Force, and they made us engineers; half of us engineers. Combat engineers. However, you know, the rapport we had among the young cats; we were just happy to be together, you know, and we went through basic and we had the band -- as I said, 45 pieces.

And we were playing the marches for the battalion, and the battalion had almost 1,000 men, and after basic, we were getting ready to go overseas, so they sent down orders; they wanted us to make the base band -- we were down at Greenwood, South Carolina, and the colonel come and talked to us, and said if they pulled us out, it would stop this whole battalion from going.

And we didn't want to be a base band. I don't want to really get in to it, but I stayed in the service from '43 to January of '46. Overseas, down in the Pacific, went to Honolulu. From Honolulu to Guam, from Guam to Okinwa, Okinwa back to the states. So I met some good musicians during that period, and that's when I started in what they called the 'new music' -- what you'd call bebop. But it was beautiful. When I come out of the service, in '46, I started working around Chicago.
